items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water in plants.

rubric.why: Identifies the theory as explaining the upward movement of water through xylem by cohesion and tension.
rubric.description: States the role of cohesion and tension in water movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking cohesion/tension with upward water movement in xylem.

rubric.why: Transpiration from leaves creates the pulling force that draws the continuous water column upward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that transpiration creates tension or pull that raises water.

modelAnswer: Cohesion-tension theory explains the upward movement of water through xylem in plants.
Transpiration from leaves creates tension (transpiration pull); cohesion between water molecules keeps the water column continuous and pulls it upward.

items.followUp: State two ways in which white blood cells protect the body.

rubric.why: Some white blood cells destroy invading microorganisms by engulfing and digesting them.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning engulfing/digesting pathogens or phagocytosis.

rubric.why: White blood cells also provide defence by producing antibodies or antitoxins and helping develop immunity.
rubric.description: Describes antibody production or immune defence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning antibodies, antitoxins, or immunity.

modelAnswer: White blood cells protect the body by engulfing and digesting pathogens (phagocytosis).
They also produce antibodies and antitoxins, helping the body develop immunity against disease.

items.followUp: Describe the cell level and organ level of biological organization.

rubric.why: The molecular level concerns atoms and molecules that form the chemical substances of living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying atoms and molecules; award 1 mark for stating that molecules form the substances/components of living organisms.

rubric.why: A tissue is formed by a group of similar cells working together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a group of similar cells; award 1 mark for stating that they perform a common function.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the tissue level.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as xylem, muscle tissue, or epithelial tissue.

modelAnswer: Molecular level: Atoms combine to form molecules, which make up the chemical substances and components of living organisms.
Tissue level: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function.
Examples of tissues include xylem, muscle tissue, and epithelial tissue.

items.followUp: Compare the cell walls and nutrition of fungi and plants.

rubric.why: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms and their cell walls contain chitin.
rubric.description: States fungal cell-wall composition or eukaryotic nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying fungi as eukaryotic or stating that their cell wall contains chitin.

rubric.why: Fungi obtain food heterotrophically, commonly by absorption, and typically reproduce by spores.
rubric.description: States a further characteristic of fungi.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct fungal characteristic such as heterotrophic nutrition, absorption of nutrients, or spore reproduction.

rubric.why: Plants are eukaryotic and generally multicellular, with cellulose cell walls.
rubric.description: Describes plant cellular organization or cell walls.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying plants as eukaryotic/multicellular or stating that their cell walls contain cellulose.

rubric.why: Plants containing chlorophyll make food by photosynthesis and are autotrophic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that plants are autotrophic or photosynthesize using chlorophyll.

rubric.why: Plants commonly store food as starch and are generally non-motile.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct additional characteristic, such as starch storage or being generally non-motile.

modelAnswer: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms; most are multicellular, and their cell walls contain chitin.
They are heterotrophic and absorb nutrients from their surroundings; many reproduce by spores.
Plants are eukaryotic and multicellular, and their cell walls contain cellulose.
Most plants contain chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis, so they are autotrophic.
Plants commonly store food as starch and are generally non-motile.

items.followUp: Explain diffusion and osmosis, and give one example of each in plants.

rubric.why: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration.
rubric.description: States the direction of movement in active transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating movement against the concentration gradient or from low to high concentration.

rubric.why: Movement against the gradient requires energy, supplied by ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning energy or ATP.

rubric.why: Membrane carrier or transport proteins help move substances across cell membranes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning transport across the membrane using carrier/transport proteins.

rubric.why: Uptake of mineral ions by root cells is a standard example of active transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mineral-ion uptake by root/root-hair cells or another valid example.

modelAnswer: Active transport is the movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, from a lower to a higher concentration.
It requires energy, usually supplied by ATP.
Carrier or transport proteins in the cell membrane help move the substances.
Root cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of enzymes and give one example.

rubric.why: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made mainly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen as the main elements.

rubric.why: Carbohydrates provide energy; glucose and starch are examples of carbohydrates.
rubric.description: States a carbohydrate function or example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct function or example.

rubric.why: Proteins contain amino acids and are composed mainly of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen.
rubric.description: States protein composition or building blocks.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying amino acids or the main elements, including nitrogen.

rubric.why: Proteins are needed for growth and repair of body tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for growth and repair or an equivalent body-building role.

rubric.why: Proteins also function as enzymes and antibodies and form important structures such as muscles.
rubric.description: Gives another protein role or example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid protein function or example.

modelAnswer: Carbohydrates are organic compounds made mainly of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
They are an important source of energy; glucose and starch are examples.
Proteins are made of amino acids and contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen.
Proteins are needed for growth and repair of body tissues.
They also form enzymes and antibodies and are important components of muscles.

items.followUp: Explain how water and minerals are transported from roots to leaves.

rubric.why: Food is transported through the phloem; this movement is called translocation.
rubric.description: Identifies the conducting tissue and process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that food moves through phloem or that the process is translocation.

rubric.why: Phloem transports dissolved organic food, especially sucrose, from sources to sinks.
rubric.description: Identifies transported food or its source-to-sink movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming sucrose/dissolved food or describing movement from source to sink.

rubric.why: Sieve tubes and companion cells are involved in phloem transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning sieve tubes or companion cells.

rubric.why: Phloem loading uses energy, and food movement can occur in different directions according to source and sink locations.
rubric.description: States an additional feature of translocation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning energy/ATP in loading or correctly noting that transport may occur in either direction.

modelAnswer: Food is transported through the phloem; this movement is called translocation.
Dissolved sugars, especially sucrose, move from sources such as leaves to sinks such as roots, fruits, or growing tissues.
Sieve tubes carry the food, and companion cells assist in its loading and transport.
Loading food into the phloem requires energy (ATP); movement may be in either direction depending on the locations of sources and sinks.

rubric.why: A species is a group of similar organisms capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a species as similar organisms that can interbreed; fertile offspring may be included.

rubric.why: A habitat is the natural place or environment in which an organism lives.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the habitat as the place or environment where an organism lives.

modelAnswer: Species: A group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
Habitat: The natural place or environment in which an organism lives.
